newsitem.title: UK: Sterling storms to fresh 4-1/2 year highs in Europe.
newsitem.headline: Sterling storms to fresh 4-1/2 year highs in Europe.

text.p: Sterling stormed to fresh 4-1/2 year peaks just shy of 2.82 marks, fuelled by a mixture of factors including lucrative UK yields, hefty U.S. buying and the European Monetary Institute's annual report, said analysts.
"The EMI's latest annual report has raised concern about the fiscal position in Europe, in general, and in Germany," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International.

Continued expectations that interest rate differentials will remain in favour of the UK relative to Germany also boosted the pound, Stamenkovic said. At 1025 GMT sterling was at 2.8190/00, just off the 2.8198 peak, its highest since September 1992.
Sterling was at its highest level since it was ejected from the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) in 1992. The pound's old ERM lower limit was 2.7780 marks.
Traders said hefty buying from the U.S. and dollar/mark strength also helped propel sterling to new peaks.
Cable also gained momentum but its rally was capped by a steamy dollar which at midday in Europe traded just below new 37-month peaks of 1.7350 marks.
At 1037 GMT sterling/dollar was trading at 1.6256/66 against 1.6213/23 in late Europe on Monday.
UK 10-year yields are among the highest in Europe and stood 185 points above their German counterparts on Tuesday.
"There's been a big buyer of sterling/mark coming out of New York. It is sterling that people want," said a senior trader at a Japanese bank.

He said UK price data released on Monday, although they were benign and reduced expectations for a sharp rise in rates, still back perceptions higher rates are needed. UK output prices fell 0.1 percent m/m in March against forecasts for a 0.1 pct rise.
"The figures still point to the need for higher rates...This is helping diversification into sterling," said the trader.
Analysts said the EMI report also helped sterling because while it seemed to dampen renewed enthusiasm for European monetary union, it was unlikely to reverse sentiment entirely.

The EMI, forerunner of the European central bank, expressed serious concerns that many European Union states have not yet managed to rein in their national deficits enough to launch the single currency in 1999.

"Anything that suggests the German budget deficit is overshooting will be perceived by the markets as increasing the likelihood of a broad-based EMU," Bank America chief economist Jeremy Hawkins said.
"It's also providing a weak mark on the increasing perception of a soft euro," added Hawkins.
"Sterling is outside the ongoing uncertainty in Europe and has consequently benefited from its safe-haven status," said DKB's Stamenkovic.
